# LaunchSense

LaunchSense checks the codebase, not the business. One lane, local. The check runs on your machine, reads your working tree including uncommitted work, and has no hourly limit. It uploads no files and no file text. What it does send outward on an online run is named under Privacy, below.

This repository is the public half: the check engine, the skill, and the installer. The policy text is served online by the vendor and reaches your tool through the policy source. The website and the policy service are not part of this repository.

Alpha has no login.

## Setup

Local reads the files. Online serves the policies. Your tool reads the rules from the policy source, guided by the skill, and the model writes the audit locally.

Local server, stdio, installed by `./install.sh` with `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT` at your checkout:

```
node <checkout>/mcp/server.ts
```

Policy source, online, static coaching material only, never a scan:

```
https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp
```

Cursor holds both entries as `launchsense` and `launchsense-policy`. Claude Code:

```
claude mcp add launchsense-policy --transport http https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp
```

The online client POSTs one JSON-RPC message and gets one JSON answer. A call is counted, with no gate.

## Installing from a coding agent

`public/install.txt` is a plain-text brief for a coding agent. It asks the person the file-read question first, then clones this repo, runs `./install.sh` with the person's repo named by `--root`, registers both servers for whichever harness it is, fetches the policy bundle once, and runs the first audit. One approval covers the whole first run.

## Tools

Online policy source, one closed and argument-free tool: `launchsense_get_policy`, which returns the whole bundle in one call. No repo URL, no file reads, no scans, no stored code. The skill fetches it once and keeps a local copy, so later runs make no policy calls and ask for no approvals. The bundle's audit instructions carry a two-level audit: Level 1 engine findings stay candidates until the named file and line is read, the audit adds a verdict and a disposition per finding, a confirmed not-real finding becomes a governance acceptance with its reason, and a local metrics table tracks per-rule precision.

Local review runs `launchsense_scan_repo` against `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT`. It takes one optional argument, `mode`: `tree` (the default) reviews the whole working tree, and `change` scopes the findings to what changed since the base of the branch and names that base, while the whole allowed tree is still read for context. OSV covers up to 50 packages. `launchsense_report` reads the latest local report under `.ls/reports`, choosing it by the saved-report filename shape, not by any `.md` file. `launchsense_github` reports the local `gh` login. `launchsense_scan_public_notice` scans nothing: it names both doors so neither is mistaken for the other.

Every report states its own completeness, in the body and the JSON, where a harness reads it: the existing `status` field is extended to `complete` or `partial`, and `statusNote` carries one line, `Review complete.` or `Review incomplete: <reasons in words>`. Completeness is per applicable check, so a check that does not apply to this repo (an npm lockfile check on a Python repo) is not a reason, and a check that applies and did not run is. The direct CLI exits 2 on an incomplete run; an explicit `--lenient` prints a warning and exits 0 instead, except for a cap hit or a lockfile in hand that was never queried, which never return 0. Over MCP the same facts arrive as report text and `isError` is reserved for a review that could not run at all. On a `change` run, an acceptance newly added to `.ls/policy.yaml` since the last report is reported as one info row naming the rule and the path: a disclosure, never above info.

A partial result is not a pass.

Governance and report consistency: in tree and change reviews, the lead, finding counts, fix plan and prompts are rebuilt from the final findings after acceptance and change filtering. Accepted findings stay named in the not-checked list but do not contribute to those recommendations. Acceptance does not change files-read counts or clear an applicable check that did not run. JSON, MCP scan output and an acknowledged saved report carry the same remaining findings and gaps; the saved report intentionally omits the tool's usage-count footer. The engine correction requires an updated checkout, not just a refreshed online policy bundle.

## Checks

Fixed checks cover secrets, code shapes, dependency names, license text, dependency license terms, and project hygiene, plus duplicate files and large files. They live in this repository: `shared/analyzers/secrets.ts` and `shared/analyzers/secretValue.ts` for credentials, `shared/analyzers/codePatterns.ts` for risky code shapes, `shared/analyzers/deps.ts` for manifests and floating versions, `shared/analyzers/licenses.ts` for license signals, `shared/analyzers/hygiene.ts` for project hygiene, `shared/review/extraChecks.ts` for duplicate and repeated content, `shared/adapters/osv.ts` for advisories, `shared/review/registry.ts` for registry facts, and `shared/policies/severity.ts` for the severity table. This is a known, fixed set, not a promise of full coverage.

## What the review reads

The local review admits at most 5,000 files and reads at most 40,000,000 actual working-tree content bytes. Ordinary whole-content analysis uses a 100,000-byte buffer limit; eligible larger files receive only the provider stream below. `package-lock.json` and names ending in `-lock.json` may exceed the per-file cap, never the remaining total budget. Binary content later skipped still consumes that byte budget. Local metadata files, such as `.ls/policy.yaml` or an `.ignore` file, are read under a separate 1 MiB bound each, so an over-bound metadata file is refused whole and disclosed. The walk does not read vendored trees (`vendor`, `third_party`, `3rdparty`, `deps`), installed packages or tool caches (`node_modules`, `.venv`, `venv`, `site-packages`, `.tox`, `.mypy_cache`, `.pytest_cache`, and the rest of the named list), or `.progress`. Binary content is not analyzed. Anything past a cap is listed as not checked.

The buffered line-level checks carry their own gates, and each one is named in the report when it fires: the secret checks do not judge lines over 2,000 characters, the code-shape checks do not judge lines over 500 characters, a file stops at 20 matched lines per file, and the per-file omission list stops at 10 rows with one count-only row for the rest, whose totals include every affected file. Those existing caps do not describe the byte-oriented provider stream.

Reads go through pinned directory handles, `/proc/self/fd` on Linux and `/dev/fd` on macOS, so other platforms are refused. A linked review root, or a linked ancestor of it, is refused before anything is read. Symbolic links inside the tree are not followed and are listed as skipped. Every child is re-checked against the directory listing by device and inode, so an entry swapped between the listing and the open is read from neither. Writes publish by rename, which is bounded rather than absolute, and no fsync is issued, so durability across a crash is not claimed.

## Large-artifact provider coverage

Larger `.html`, `.htm`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs` and `.cjs` files can receive only a supported provider-signature stream, with a 64 KiB read buffer and deterministic path sorting. Streamed reads consume the same 5,000 admitted files and 40,000,000 actual bytes as buffered reads, not extra budgets. Other large extensions remain whole-skipped; the lockfile exception is unchanged.

The supported shapes are `AKIA` plus 16 uppercase letters or digits; `ghp_`, `gho_`, `ghu_`, `ghs_` or `ghr_` plus 20 alphanumeric characters; `github_pat_` plus 20 letters, digits or underscores; and six standard private-key BEGIN labels (generic, RSA, EC, DSA, OPENSSH, ENCRYPTED). These are shape signals, not proof of live credentials. Generic credentials, code shapes, repeated functions and other whole-content checks do not run on these large files. Their `artifactCoverage` records keep those families `Not checked`, so the overall review remains `Partial` after a complete provider stream.

Provider coverage is `Checked` only for a complete stable read, `Partial` for a judged prefix, `Not checked` when the byte budget permits no provider bytes judged, or `Unknown` after a read error, mutation or NUL binary content. Invalidated observations are discarded. Detection continues after 20 listed hits with a known withheld counter; matched values and snippets are not returned. Streamed `byteOffset` is zero-based, line is one-based LF and column is a one-based UTF-8 byte column. A full artifact SHA requires a complete stable read. JSON carries `artifactCoverage`, `streamedProviderSummary`, `artifactIdentities` and listed `artifactSignals`. Saved text preserves safe coordinates and hashes and labels signals not raised after scope filtering or governance. Neither an unraised signal nor a full hash is clearance.

Pull a newer engine checkout to install this path; refreshing the coaching bundle alone does not install it. It uses Node builtins, adds no dependencies, executes no target code and makes no network requests. The Node version guard is not an operating-system sandbox. Linux is verified; macOS is allowed but unverified and other platforms are refused. These signals do not guarantee security and are not SOC 2/ISO certification. Do not claim all vulnerabilities are found.

## Privacy

The hosted policy source receives no repository source: its one tool takes no arguments, so there is nothing to send. Nothing here claims that no data ever leaves the machine, because that would be false. On an online run the engine sends:

- to OSV, the ecosystem, name, and version of lockfile packages, at most 50 per run;
- to deps.dev and ClearlyDefined, the package name and version, at most 15 non-dev packages per run;
- to OpenSSF Scorecard, the `github.com/owner/repo` slug, only when `package.json` names one;
- to the engine's optional decision lane, only when it is switched on. `shared/adapters/decision.ts` names the providers: a local Ollama model, a development instrument that is off unless `LAUNCHSENSE_LOCAL_DECISION=1` is set, which needs no key, TypeSafe at api.typesafe.ai, which runs when `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is set, and Perplexity at api.perplexity.ai, which runs when `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY` is set. The installer sets neither the switch nor a key, so by default the engine makes no model request. The local rung's default address is loopback on this machine, and `LAUNCHSENSE_LOCAL_DECISION_URL` can point it elsewhere, so a local run is not guaranteed to stay on the machine. When the reorder path runs, its state carries the finding title, severity, and rule id, and a title can itself contain a file path, a line number, a host name, or a package name and version; the question keys are hash-derived, so the raw fingerprint is not sent. The unknown-next-look path sends only a fixed choice list and nothing about the repo;
- local audit usage counts are not sent to LaunchSense. The sender is retired, even with an old opt-in or a configured endpoint.

Nothing else leaves the machine, and the policy fetch carries nothing about your repo. The model that writes the audit is the model your coding harness is configured with, on your provider. That inference is separate from this engine: its privacy depends on your harness and provider, and nothing this installer sets chooses it. The engine's decision lane above is operator configuration, not your harness's model. Removing the usage sender does not disable these calls; the switch that covers the engine calls is `LAUNCHSENSE_OFFLINE=1`.

`LAUNCHSENSE_OFFLINE=1` disables the engine's outbound calls for the run. It does not control your coding harness's network use or its separately approved policy fetch; use the cached coaching copy for an offline review.

The installer asks only the agent-file/report question: whether it may read the agent instruction files and save the local report copy, default yes; ordinary project files are read only for a review the person asks for. It preserves historical usage decisions in `~/.config/launchsense/consent.jsonl` byte-for-byte and writes no new usage grant, refusal or withdrawal. The acknowledgement is keyed to notice version `2026-10-14`, so an answer given for the older, broader wording is not applied to it. Compatibility fields in `~/.config/launchsense/config.json` keep usage off; they are not new consent decisions.

The terminal report says `Usage counts were not sent.` JSON always reports `diagnosticsSent: false` with the closed reason `diagnosticsReason: "disabled"`. Old opt-ins and `LAUNCHSENSE_API_URL` do not reactivate the sender. The saved report copy carries no usage-count line and no model quote.

## The `.ls` files

The review keeps its own state in a `.ls` folder under `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT`. The folder is gitignored and stays on the machine.

`.ls/policy.yaml` is the repo's own memory: the findings a person already accepted, each with a reason, so a later review does not raise them again. It is read once per run, before the walk, and the single read is shared by every later step. It is parsed in full and it is declarative only: no code, no anchors, no includes, no wildcards, and it cannot disable a rule or change a severity. Tab indentation, multiple documents, anchors or aliases, an unsupported version, and unknown keys are refused whole rather than half-read. An absent file changes nothing. A link, an unreadable file, or a file over the 1 MiB metadata bound is a refusal, never a silent absence. A wrong file is refused whole and nothing is suppressed. A file that would silence more than half the findings through one acceptance, or four fifths in total, is refused whole. An accepted finding is removed from the findings list and named in the not-checked list as accepted, so a suppression is never silent. An acceptance is written only after the person confirms the entry.

`.ls/reports/` holds one saved copy per acknowledged run, all named from the run's own timestamp:

- the report, `<stamp>.md`, where the stamp is the ISO time with its colons and dots replaced by hyphens;
- the policy snapshot, `<stamp>.policy.yaml`, the exact bytes that were read, or an empty policy recorded when the file was absent, and nothing at all when the read was refused;
- the third-party notice, `<stamp>-THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.generated.md`.

The first time the review writes `.ls/`, it adds one `.ls/` line to `.gitignore`, after the file-read acknowledgement, and says so when it cannot. It writes nothing else in your repo and never edits source code.

## The report

The report leads with the solution, not a wall of findings: START HERE, then the lead fix prompt and the next prompts to paste, each naming the file; then PLAN, the ordered fix steps, secrets first, each with its why, files, and checklist; then DETAIL, the findings, the not-checked list line for line, the licence suggestion, and one line pointing at the third-party notice file written beside the report. The notice text is not dumped into the report body.

## Ignoring files

Three sources exclude a path before it is read, and each skip is disclosed with its source. `.gitignore` is honoured through real Git, so nested files, negation, and directory rules are Git's own semantics, never a re-implementation. Outside a Git work tree, the Git side is not applied and is named as not applied, nothing is invented on its behalf, and a genuine non-Git folder is read normally because there is no `.gitignore` contract to preserve there. When Git cannot establish which paths are ignored (a failed or inconsistent lookup, a reply larger than the 16 MiB git stdout bound, a git binary that cannot be run, or a git that refuses for another reason), the walk reads no repository content at all, and the run is partial; a git binary that cannot be run is not reported as a non-Git folder; that refusal bounds the walk only, so the review's own metadata inputs are still read and a walker file count of zero is not zero metadata reads. `.ignore` files are honoured for a documented subset only: comment lines, blank lines, and one clean segment per line naming a file or directory under that file's own folder. Glob characters, negation, anchored or slashed paths, and whitespace-bearing names are not honoured, and the report says so when it applies. A link, an unreadable file, or a file over the 1 MiB bound is refused or withheld, and exclusion discovery descends only through a directory observed and then opened successfully (a listing or open that fails after observation withholds that scope), so the paths it might have excluded are not read.

## The licence declaration

For a project that commits an npm `package-lock.json` with a `packages` map, every installed package, direct and transitive, is read for the licence it declares, and the review writes a third-party notice file named `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.generated.md`: the same lockfile gives the same bytes. Where the lockfile has no `license` field and an installed `package.json` is available, that manifest is the fallback, and a lockfile that disagrees with it reads as Unknown. A declaration that is not an SPDX expression, such as `MIT/X11`, reads as Unknown. `UNLICENSED` reads as `LicenseRef-Proprietary-UNLICENSED`. An `OR` expression stays a choice. A bare `GPL-2.0` is kept as declared and marked deprecated. `GPL-2.0+` normalizes to `GPL-2.0-or-later`.

`shared/licensing/obligations.ts` holds one cited row per licence family: licence text, copyright notice, a NOTICE file where the licence has one, state of changes, source disclosure for copyleft, and the distribution clash for strong copyleft. It is a table of what a licence text asks for. It is not a legal engine, and it does not decide whether an obligation applies to how you ship.

Not checked on any surface: yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, Cargo, Go and PyPI dependency licences, a vendored tree, a per-file SPDX header or REUSE.toml, and registry freshness. A lockfile with no `packages` map reads as incomplete, not as zero licences.

A licence document is a recognised licence basename (LICENSE, LICENCE, COPYING, NOTICE, and their `LICENSE-MIT`/`MIT-LICENSE`/`LICENSE.md` forms) with no extension or a plain document extension (`.md`, `.txt`, `.rst`, `.html`, and the like). `COPYING.LESSER` and `COPYING.LIB` are also recognised documents. Known source kinds, including `.mjs`, `.zig` and `.jl`, stay in the code and secret lanes; their quoted licence text does not set aggregate policy. Unsupported root licensing inputs (such as `LICENSE.spdx`, `LICENSE.custom` or `LICENSE.json`) and listed-but-unread root documents remain unresolved, with a not-checked coverage row; a MIT manifest elsewhere cannot make them whole-project `Allowed`/mirror. Scope-limiting wording needs review; unsupported or contradictory scope statements remain `Unknown`, never a fabricated grant or restriction. Local negation is not a whole-document override. These bounded static patterns examine all supplied licence content, not only the first 4,000 characters, within the existing caller read limits (ordinary files: 100,000 bytes; global limits remain unchanged). This is not legal clearance, and a person reads the terms.

Filename evidence is not content permission. The licensing lane keeps already-discovered root licensing names from directory/Git listings and exact skip/stream metadata separate from admitted content. Ignored, refused, linked, oversized, unreadable, binary or provider-only licensing candidates retain their original unread provenance in one unresolved row per root name. No filename is invented from skip prose or an exclusion declaration, and no excluded scope is opened to search for licensing. The admitted-files count and the existing 100,000 bytes per ordinary file, 40,000,000 global bytes and 5,000 admitted-file limits are unchanged. With other content admitted, a known unread root cannot be replaced by a permissive manifest: Unknown/reference-only and its medium policy finding remain. With no content admitted, the existing Not checked/info policy remains, alongside the named unresolved coverage and incomplete status.

Scope checks recognise a bounded vocabulary of grant/scope/coverage cues and only/exclusive/limited/restricted/sole qualifiers. Recognised qualifiers outside supported phrase forms remain unresolved rather than permissive. Local negation has three states: positive, negated or unresolved; supported scope modifiers may intervene, but an unhandled local negation is not a confirmed positive restriction. Liability/obligation roles are distinguished by bounded clause rules, not by a bare licence word or file path. Those rules are not general language understanding or legal interpretation, and unrecognised arbitrary wording is not cleared.

Scope role and negation checks use the same local predicate boundaries. Match bodies and qualifier ownership are confined to one predicate range partitioned before matching. Commas, colons, semicolons, sentence punctuation and the supported conjunctions separate predicates; scope-label colons and explicit path-only continuations remain within their owning grant. Plain quoted path tokens and path components named like conjunctions are not mistaken for new predicates. An unrelated predicate cannot erase another predicate's unresolved evidence, and a negated match cannot own a later predicate's qualifiers. These are bounded lexical forms, not general language understanding. Git discovery keeps all validated untracked candidates independently of ignore classification, including when classification later fails or an observed entry disappears. A failed or malformed candidate listing contributes no names; the existing NUL/path validation and 16 MiB output bound remain. Retaining an observed name is not an atomic filesystem snapshot, proof of current contents or permission to open excluded content.

The local `gh` metadata commands each have a 10-second deadline, independent of child stream closure, and a combined 65,536-byte stdout/stderr allowance. Failed exits, timeouts, overflow, malformed fields and non-boolean privacy stay unavailable errors, not “not logged in,” “No current repo” or “public.” Only valid ordinary metadata is rendered; supported credential spans are refused even beside identifier characters. This stricter output guard does not change repository secret detection. The command budget is per command, not a 10-second budget for all three commands together.

License lines are signals, not legal advice. Unknown stays unknown. A model may quote one next look. That quote is not a finding. The priority table always orders the report, and a decision lane may reorder inside one severity band. The model does not choose which findings exist.

## What the AI does and does not decide

Two paths reach a model on this engine, both through the decision lane in `shared/adapters/decision.ts`, and both run only when the lane is switched on: `LAUNCHSENSE_LOCAL_DECISION=1` turns on the local rung and needs no key, and a hosted rung runs when `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` or `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY` is set. The installer sets neither, so the default is no model request at all. Both paths are soft: a failed lane changes nothing and the run continues.

- `ordering` reorders findings that already exist, inside one severity band. `shared/adapters/decision.ts`, `shared/reports/priority.ts`. The reorder state carries the finding title, severity, and rule id, and the question carries the title inline, so a title that holds a file path, a line number, a host name, or a package coordinate carries that. The question keys are hash-derived from the fingerprint, so the raw fingerprint is not sent. The report states the provenance in plain words, then the order source and the count of positions a lane moved.
- `unknownNext` picks one next-look sentence for an unknown gap, from a fixed list. `shared/review/unknownQuote.ts`. It sends a fixed choice list and no repository text. The quote is not a finding and does not turn an unknown into a licence or a pass.

The guarded licence lookup for an Unknown licence exists in `shared/licensing/lookup.ts` and is refused unless a lane is configured; its answer is a suggestion, never a licence fact. The lane is injected by the caller, holds no key, and is not wired on this path, so nothing is asked. If a lane were supplied, the prompt would carry only the package name and version with fixed wording. The `humanOversightLevel` is `prompt_guided` in every case, which in C2PA Technical Specification 2.4 means a person provided the request and nobody approved the output. No path here is `fully_autonomous` and none is `human_validated`. The vocabulary is borrowed and this is not a conformance claim.

The AI never decides a finding, a severity, a licence fact, consent, who a caller is, or whether a request is allowed. Each of those is fixed code: `shared/analyzers`, `shared/policies/severity.ts`, `shared/licensing`, `install.sh`.

## Fetching and refreshing the policy

The skill fetches the bundle once and keeps the copy in the skill folder. Later runs read that copy and make no policy calls. Refresh only when the person asks for it, or when the person has approved an online fetch. There is no automatic version comparison without a call and no auto-update: a coaching change reaches you on the fetch you were asked to make, and a detector change is a code change that reaches you when this repo is pulled.

## Analytics

A call to the policy source is counted on the server, because the call is to our service. No gate is placed on it. The current route records closed method/tool/outcome labels and a fixed `unknown` client label, not repository source. Local audits send no usage counts. Recorded initialization events are not unique users or proven unique sessions. The vendor's read-only statistics command is not shipped in this engine-only repository. No PII is claimed as a proven property of provider logs or retained production rows.

## Do not claim

The review does not say the app will sell. It does not edit the repo. It does not certify anything, and it is not a compliance badge. It does not treat a source-available license as open source. It does not say nothing leaves the machine: name the outbound calls instead. It does not promise full coverage: the checks are the fixed analyzers in this repository.
